title: The Shared Meal: the Farmhouse at Moscia, the Eranos Table, and the Archive of Archetypal Images
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: London, the engineer's daughter born
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and month; the day is contested. English-language sources, including English Wikipedia and the ARAS Connections newsletter, give 19 October 1881; some German-language references give 18 October. Unresolved in everything reachable, and not adjudicated here. The father's employer is corrected: the dossier said Westinghouse Brake and Signal Company, which was formed by merger only in 1920; English Wikipedia says Westinghouse Air Brake Company, verbatim.
stops.campa: Albertus Philippus Kapteyn comes to London in 1881 for the Westinghouse Air Brake Company and by 1887 runs its London site. His wife Geertruida Muysken, called Truus, is a Dutch feminist and social reformer who keeps a house full of argument. Their eldest child is born in that first London autumn and named Olga. She has two Dutch parents and an English birth certificate, and her working life will be spent in Italian-speaking Switzerland. English sources give the nineteenth of October for the birth, some German ones the eighteenth. The day has never been settled.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 89
suggested_refs: Westinghouse Air Brake Company records for the London site, 1881-1887

stops.name: North London Collegiate School, the schoolroom on Sandall Road
stops.date_confidence: attested that she attended; the years are inferred from her birth date and no source gives them. Coordinate corrected: the intake pool pinned Camden Town station, 51.539/-0.1425. The school occupied Sandall Road from 1879 until the Canons Park move in 1929, which is the site a pupil of the 1890s attended. A claim about family darkroom work with a photographer father was attached to this stop in the pool, cited to English Wikipedia; it is not in that article and no source for it was found, so it is dropped.
stops.campa: Frances Mary Buss's school on Sandall Road examines its girls as if they were boys, which in the 1890s is a position and not a convenience. Here an education is an entitlement rather than an ornament, at an age when Olga Kapteyn is too young to know the point is contested. She passes through in those years, and so does a schoolfellow named Marie Stopes, who will spend her adult life arguing about contraception in public. What Olga read there, and how well she did, is recorded nowhere at all.
suggested_refs: North London Collegiate School registers for the Sandall Road years

stops.name: Zürich, the family goes south
stops.date_confidence: attested that the family relocated to Zürich by the end of the nineteenth century; no source gives a year, and 1895 is a placeholder to order the segment. The corpus Zürich placeholder pin is used. The dossier's further claim that Truus Muysken's Zürich circle connected to George Bernard Shaw and Peter Kropotkin could not be confirmed by any reachable source and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Before the century turns the Kapteyns leave England for Zürich, and Truus opens there the same kind of house she kept in London: reform-minded, argumentative, full of people intending to change how everybody lives. Her daughter learns the country on skis and on rope, climbing. The Zürich of the 1890s is a clearing-house for Lebensreform, for the anarchists and vegetarians and dress reformers moving between Munich and the Alps, and the girl grows up inside that traffic without having chosen it.
suggested_refs: Truus Muysken's Zürich reform circle, 1890s

stops.name: Zürich, the School of Applied Arts
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of entry. The coordinate is a declared placeholder: it is the Ausstellungsstrasse building now called the Museum für Gestaltung, which opened only in 1933 and is therefore not where she studied. Where the Kunstgewerbeschule was housed in 1900 is not established in any reachable source. The intake pool's 47.3823/8.5309 was neither the study site nor the modern building.
stops.campa: At nineteen she enters the Kunstgewerbeschule and is taught the trades of the hand: sewing, embroidery, jewelry, design. It is training in making objects rather than in discussing them, and the mark of it stays on her for sixty years, in an institution assembled out of houses, folders, boxes, mounted photographs and typed programmes rather than out of a doctrine. Where the school stood in 1900 nobody now records; the building that carries its name today was not raised until 1933.
suggested_refs: Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich enrolment records, 1900

stops.name: University of Zürich, three years of art history
stops.date_confidence: attested for the study and the span 1906-1909. Whether she completed a degree is not established by any accessible source, and none denies one either; the gap is left open rather than filled in either direction.
stops.campa: From 1906 to 1909 she reads the history of art at the university on the slope above the Limmat. Whether she took a degree is established by nothing, and denied by nothing. What the three years give her is a professional habit with pictures: dated, attributed, compared, filed, and it will outlast every other part of her training. She is free in a way that almost no woman of her generation is free, the daughter of a rich engineer with no need of a wage. She leaves the university in 1909, unmarried, twenty-seven.
suggested_refs: University of Zürich matriculation records, 1906-1909

segments.name: The Marriage and the Field East of Vienna

stops.name: Zürich, marriage to Iwan Fröbe
stops.date_confidence: the year 1909 is attested by English Wikipedia and by AWARE. His nationality is contested and is not resolved here: English Wikipedia calls him the Croatian-Austrian flutist and conductor Iwan Fröbe; German Wikipedia calls him an Austrian conductor and musician of Slovenian descent, with dates 1880-1915. No month or day is recorded anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: In 1909 she marries Iwan Hermann Fröbe, a flautist and conductor in Zürich's orchestral world, and takes the double name she carries for the remaining fifty-three years of her life. He is born in 1880, a year before her, and the marriage will last six years and end in a field east of Vienna. His origins do not resolve: one account calls him Croatian-Austrian, another Austrian of Slovenian descent, and the two stand unreconciled in the record. Of the wedding itself nothing is recorded anywhere consulted except the year.
suggested_refs: Zürich marriage register, 1909

stops.name: Braunschweig, following the orchestra
stops.date_confidence: tradition, single tertiary source. English Wikipedia carries the German years without an itinerary; the sequence of cities varies between short biographies and is corroborated by no document. The date is a placeholder to order the segment.
stops.campa: The conductor's engagements set the itinerary now. Short biographies place the couple at Braunschweig in the first years of the marriage, but the sequence of German cities varies between accounts and no document fixes it. Whatever she made in these years, embroidery or drawing or nothing at all, no catalogue holds it. She is in her late twenties, keeping house in a language she has and a country she does not know, one orchestral season at a time.
suggested_refs: Braunschweig orchestral personnel lists, 1909-1910

stops.name: Munich, a period nobody dates
stops.date_confidence: tradition. English Wikipedia and AWARE both mention Munich and both hedge; AWARE says only that she visited with her husband. No duration, address or purpose is given anywhere consulted.
stops.campa: Munich comes before Berlin, for a stretch that nobody dates. The city in 1910 runs on the same enthusiasms as her mother's Zürich rooms: Schwabing, vegetarianism, dress reform, Eastern books read closely by people who have never been east, the whole apparatus that will shortly come down over the Alps and put up huts on a hill above Ascona. She passes through as a conductor's wife. Her Munich months amount to one hedged line in each of two short biographies.
suggested_refs: Schwabing Lebensreform circles, c. 1910

stops.name: Berlin, the Needle
stops.date_confidence: attested. AWARE states it directly: Berlin period, collaborated with philologist André Jolles on the Nadel sewing circle, established 1911. The intake pool's chronology lens tagged this a reconstruction while its geography lens tagged it attested from the same source; the attested reading is taken.
stops.campa: In Berlin she works with the philologist André Jolles, who founds in 1911 a sewing circle he calls Nadel, the Needle. Dress reform is her mother's household politics carried onto the body, and this is the first work of Olga's own hands that any record names. She is thirty. The garments are cut after classical Greek models and made entirely by hand, worn in daylight by people who hold that the corset is a political object, and Olga embroiders and embellishes them: Greek lines in linen, stitched at a table in Berlin.
suggested_refs: André Jolles and the Nadel dress-reform circle, Berlin, founded 1911

stops.name: Gersau, on the Vierwaldstättersee
stops.date_confidence: single source and no dates. The aras.org newsletter mentions a period of residence at Gersau during the marriage; nothing else consulted repeats it, no house is identified, no duration given. The date orders the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: For some part of the marriage the Fröbes live at Gersau on the Vierwaldstättersee, under the wooded slope, across the water from the Rütli meadow where the old confederates are said to have sworn. It sits in the record the way a photograph sits in a drawer with nothing written on the back. The second half of her life will be spent on a different Swiss lake, in a house she almost never leaves. One account mentions Gersau once. No dates, no house, no duration, no reason.
suggested_refs: Gersau, Vierwaldstättersee, residence during the Fröbe marriage

stops.name: Zürich, the Table Ronde
stops.date_confidence: the salon is attested: English Wikipedia names it, and German Wikipedia independently records that she maintained a literary salon in Zurich during the First World War. The specific 1914 starting date rests on weaker sourcing than the salon itself, and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: War closes the frontiers and the couple come back to Zürich, a city filling with exiles, refusers, and the young men who will shortly invent Dada in a tavern off the Spiegelgasse. Olga opens a salon and calls it the Table Ronde. She chooses who is admitted, she sets what is discussed, she feeds them, she keeps the evening moving. Nineteen years before Eranos the form is already finished, and only the subject has not arrived. When exactly she began it is less firmly attested than the salon itself.
suggested_refs: The Table Ronde salon, Zürich, First World War years

stops.name: Zürich, the twins
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month. English Wikipedia dates the birth of twin daughters to May 1915. The city is probable rather than documented; no source consulted names the house, the street, or the daughters.
stops.campa: Twin daughters are born in May 1915. The city is almost certainly Zürich, though no source consulted names the house or the street. Their father is in Austria-Hungary, attached to an air arm four years old, flying machines that kill their own crews at a rate no ministry publishes. Olga is thirty-three, with two newborns and a husband in uniform, in a neutral country with the war on every side of it. Nobody records the daughters' names. Who raised them, and where, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Zürich birth register, May 1915

stops.name: Fischamend, the crash
stops.date_confidence: attested as to place and month: English Wikipedia says a plane crash in September 1915 in Fischamend near Vienna, and the ARAS newsletter confirms she was widowed in September 1915. The intake dossier wrongly hedged Fischamend as unconfirmed. What is genuinely unconfirmed is the detail, repeated in the literature, that he was testing an aerial camera for the Austro-Hungarian military: no source consulted, English or German, mentions a camera. No day of the month is recorded.
stops.campa: At Fischamend, on the flat ground east of Vienna where the Austro-Hungarian air troops keep their field, Iwan Fröbe is killed in a crash in September 1915, aged thirty-five. The place, the month and the aircraft are attested. The detail everyone repeats, that he was testing an aerial camera for the military, appears in no source consulted and stands unsupported. Olga is a widow of thirty-three with infant twins. Four years pass before anyone records anything further of her at all.
suggested_refs: Austro-Hungarian Fliegerarsenal at Fischamend, accident records 1915

segments.name: The Hill, the Farmhouse, and the Hall Built Early

stops.name: Monte Verità, the cure above Ascona
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay, by AWARE, by the ARAS newsletter and by English Wikipedia; the month is not given and the date orders the segment. The pin is the canonical corpus Monte Verità coordinate, inherited byte-identical from ida_hoffmann.journey.json. The sanatorium of 1919 is institutionally distinct from the earlier colony on the same hill.
stops.campa: She comes up the hill above Ascona with her father, for a course of natural treatment. Monte Verità has by 1919 run through its vegetarian colony, its light-and-air huts, its barefoot dancers and its analysts, and is passing into the hands of people who mean to operate it as a sanatorium. She takes the sun, the diet, the air. From the terrace the lake road can be seen running west toward Ronco, past farmhouses standing empty on the shore at Moscia.
suggested_refs: Monte Verità sanatorium, Ascona, treatment registers c. 1919

stops.name: Moscia, Casa Gabriella
stops.date_confidence: attested as her lifelong home; the year is contested. German Wikipedia dates the acquisition to 1919, immediately after the Monte Verità stay; AWARE and English Wikipedia give 1920. The transaction is contested too: accounts differ over whether her father bought it for her or she acquired it from an ophthalmologist named Hoffmann with paternal inheritance. The pin is the canonical corpus Eranos-house coordinate inherited byte-identical from jung.journey.json; independent checking against the Eranos Foundation address at Via Moscia 125 and swisstopo suggests roughly 46.1518/8.7528 for the house itself, but the canon is kept so the pin does not split across the corpus.
stops.campa: She takes Casa Gabriella, an old farmhouse on the Ascona shore at Moscia, with her father's money, and does not move house again for forty-two years. The lake is at the door and the terraces climb behind, and the room that will one day be filled to the ceiling with photographs is her bedroom. The sources divide on the year, 1919 or 1920, and on the transaction: whether Albertus bought it for her, or she bought it out of what he left, or it came from an ophthalmologist named Hoffmann. None of the three is proven.
suggested_refs: Casa Gabriella, Via Moscia, Ascona, home from 1919 or 1920 until her death

stops.name: Moscia, the years of reading
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from a single source. The seven-year period of solitary study, the encounter with the I Ching and the meeting with its translator Richard Wilhelm all rest on the aras.org ARAS Connections newsletter alone and appear in none of the sources that could be read directly in this pass. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: For something like seven years she reads: Indian philosophy, Theosophy, yoga, meditation, comparative religion, the whole shelf that Europe has been assembling out of translated fragments since the 1880s. She does not read them as literature. What is certain is the arrangement, a widow alone in a lakeside farmhouse with two daughters and a private income. The account of the retreat rests on one institutional source, as do the encounter with the I Ching and the meeting with its translator Richard Wilhelm.
suggested_refs: Richard Wilhelm's I Ching translation, Jena 1924

stops.name: Darmstadt, Keyserling's School of Wisdom
stops.date_confidence: the contact with Hermann Keyserling's circle in the 1920s is attested by English Wikipedia; the year here is a placeholder. That she met Jung at Darmstadt around 1930 is Eranos institutional memory and is confirmed by no source consulted, in respect of the meeting, the place or the year. The pin is the corpus Darmstadt School of Wisdom coordinate shared by keyserling.journey.json and martin_buber.journey.json.
stops.campa: Hermann Keyserling's School of Wisdom at Darmstadt is the thing she is going to build, made ten years earlier and in a German provincial capital: scholars from incompatible disciplines gathered periodically under an annual theme, and a founder who convenes rather than lectures. She makes contact with the circle in the twenties. That she met Jung at Darmstadt around 1930 is Ascona's own institutional memory, carried on repetition and on nothing else. No source consulted confirms the meeting, the place or the year.
suggested_refs: Hermann Keyserling's Schule der Weisheit, Darmstadt, programmes of the 1920s

stops.name: Marburg, the ecumenical circle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia carries a brief mention of contact with the Marburg ecumenical circle in the 1920s; nothing establishes a personal visit as against correspondence, and no year is given. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Among the contacts of her twenties is the ecumenical circle at Marburg, theologians working across confessional lines at a moment when that is a position with enemies rather than a courtesy. She is building a correspondence rather than a career, and the names in it are the names that will come down the lake road in August after August. The record amounts to a single brief mention. Nothing in it establishes that she went to Marburg rather than wrote to it.
suggested_refs: The Marburg ecumenical circle of the 1920s

stops.name: Moscia, the hall built before the reason for it
stops.date_confidence: the 1928 build year is attested by Tevebring in the Public Domain Review and by English Wikipedia; no month is given. That Rudolf Otto suggested the name Eranos is attested by English Wikipedia. Canonical corpus pin, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: Above the farmhouse she puts up a second building: a hall with a lectern, a terrace, a roof over an audience that does not exist. She has no conference, no programme and no name for one. What she has is a plan for a study centre, an ashram in her own word, and enough money to build the room first. The religious historian Rudolf Otto supplies the name afterward: Eranos, the shared meal to which each guest brings a dish. The hall waits five years for its first speaker.
sources: Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: Casa Eranos, the lecture hall on the Casa Gabriella property, built 1928

segments.name: The Meditation Plates and the Summer School

stops.name: Moscia, the Meditation Plates
stops.date_confidence: attested. Sugden dates the Meditation Plate series c. 1926-34, citing Fröbe-Kapteyn 1932. The Metropolitan Museum's complete set of fourteen Theosophical Prints is dated by the museum to circa 1930; its accession year, given in the intake dossier as 2023, could not be verified, the Met catalogue page returning HTTP 429 in both research passes.
stops.campa: Between 1926 and 1934 she paints the series she calls Meditation Plates: hard geometry, mandalas, ascending and radiating forms in tempera, India ink and gold leaf on cardboard. They are instruments rather than pictures, made to be looked at inside a practice, and they belong to her Theosophical years. Decades after her death a complete set of the fourteen related prints enters the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, catalogued there as Theosophical Prints and dated by the museum to about 1930.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 89-94
suggested_refs: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Complete Set of Theosophical Prints, ca. 1930, accession 900081
Centre Pompidou, Women in Abstraction, Paris, 2021

stops.name: Connecticut, the proposal to Alice Bailey
stops.date_confidence: the 1930 visit is attested by Sugden, p. 91, citing Bailey's Unfinished Autobiography, 216. Sugden names only the state. The coordinate is a declared placeholder on Stamford, where Bailey's work was based; the intake pool's 41.3/-73.4 was open country near Redding associated with nobody. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: She crosses the Atlantic to put a proposal to Alice Bailey, whose Arcane School commands a Theosophical readership on two continents: a spiritual centre at Ascona-Moscia, non-sectarian, deliberately open to the people the existing occult schools exclude from one another. Bailey records the visit in her autobiography, and Olga sails home with a collaborator and a summer school. The town is named in nothing consulted, and Stamford, where Bailey's work was based, stands here only as a marker.
stops.quote: spiritual centre... open to esoteric thinkers and occult students of all groups in Europe and elsewhere
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, reported in Alice A. Bailey, The Unfinished Autobiography (Lucis, 1973), 216, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 91
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 91
suggested_refs: Alice A. Bailey, The Unfinished Autobiography (1973)

stops.name: Moscia, the summer school
stops.date_confidence: attested for the years 1930 to 1932; the month is a placeholder. The name is genuinely unsettled and is not resolved here: the archival report of the first session is headed International Center for Spiritual Research (Bailey and Fröbe-Kapteyn 1930, HS1016:299 49, C. G. Jung Papers, ETH Zürich); English Wikipedia's Alice Bailey article calls it the School of Spiritual Research; Spiritual Centre is Sugden's own descriptive phrase, which the intake dossier mistook for the body's name. Canonical corpus pin.
stops.campa: For three summers, from 1930 to 1932, the hall on the property holds a school run jointly with Bailey. What it is called depends on which document is in front of you: the report of its first session heads itself International Center for Spiritual Research, later accounts call it the School of Spiritual Research, its historian calls it simply a Spiritual Centre. What it does is not in dispute. People come from several countries to sit in one room on a private shore and be addressed on a single theme.
stops.quote: We are gathered here not for the satisfaction of personal curiosity, but in the spirit of a joint enterprise, a work dedicated to the development of a new consciousness.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn and Alice Bailey, joint declaration, 1930, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 91
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 91
suggested_refs: Report of First Session, International Center for Spiritual Research, 1930, HS1016:299 49, ETH Zürich

stops.name: Moscia, Die Verkündigung
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by Sugden's figure caption, which also corrects the medium: the intake dossier called it a colour screenprint, and the caption reads tempera, India ink and gold leaf on cardboard. The screenprint attribution appears to come from confusion with the separate Theosophical Prints of about 1930, which are colour silkscreen. No month is recorded.
stops.campa: In 1932 she makes Die Verkündigung, the Annunciation: tempera, India ink and gold leaf on cardboard, geometry standing where the angel and the girl would stand. It belongs to the Meditation Plate series, and it is among the last things she paints before the conferences take her hands. Catalogues have sometimes called it a screenprint, confusing it with the colour silkscreen Theosophical Prints of about 1930. The sheet itself is painted, and it is filed today in the picture archive at Küsnacht.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), fig. 3 caption
suggested_refs: Die Verkündigung, 1932, item 0.35BIBO, Folder 35002, C. G. Jung-Institut Bildarchiv, Küsnacht

stops.name: Moscia, the break with Bailey
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year: Tevebring dates the rupture to 1932, Sugden frames the collaboration as running until 1932, and English Wikipedia's Alice Bailey article says the school closed in 1932 over personal conflict. The month is a placeholder and the substance of the quarrel is described in no source consulted beyond the word personal. Canonical corpus pin.
stops.campa: The partnership ends in 1932, in a quarrel that the surviving accounts describe with the single word personal. Bailey goes, the school closes, and Olga keeps the hall, the shore, the correspondence and the idea. What she does next is not a continuation but a substitution: where the summer school had doctrine and adepts, the thing that replaces it will have philologists, orientalists, historians of religion and a psychiatrist, and no doctrine that anybody in the room is required to hold. She is fifty.
sources: Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 91
suggested_refs: The closure of the Ascona summer school, 1932

stops.name: Küsnacht, the turn to Jung
stops.date_confidence: the relationship is attested from about 1930 onward and the iconographic commissions from 1934 to 1938 are attested by AWARE and by Sugden, p. 92. The specific date here orders the segment and asserts nothing; where and when they first met is not established, see the Darmstadt stop. The holding of roughly 6,500 copies of her Archive images in the Jung Institute Bildarchiv is attested by Sugden.
stops.campa: The house on the lake at Küsnacht holds the man who reorganizes her project. Jung gives her a vocabulary in which collecting pictures counts as research rather than as devotion: archetype, active imagination, the collective unconscious. From about 1930 she is inside his orbit, and through the whole of the following decade she sends him iconographic material for his work on alchemy. The picture archive of the Jung Institute at Küsnacht will end up holding some six thousand five hundred copies of her images.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 92
suggested_refs: C. G. Jung-Institut Bildarchiv, Küsnacht, copies of the Eranos Archive

stops.name: Casa Eranos, the first Tagung
stops.date_confidence: attested. The August 1933 date and the theme Yoga und Meditation im Osten und im Westen are given by Sugden, p. 90, and corroborated by AWARE and English Wikipedia. The precise day and the pin are inherited byte-identical from jung.journey.json, the corpus's canonical record of this scene. The quote is from her own 1941 correspondence and is placed here for what it says about the form, not as words spoken in 1933.
stops.campa: In August 1933 the hall she built five years early is used for what it was built for. She has set the theme herself, Yoga und Meditation im Osten und im Westen, written to the speakers, arranged their lodging, ordered the food, timed the sessions, and she will take the papers away to be printed. Jung lectures. The audience sits under the cedars between the hall and the water. She does not speak from that lectern this year, nor in any of the twenty-eight years that follow.
stops.quote: The speakers at every meeting are a unit, bound by their individual relationship to the central theme and to that dynamic force that we call Eranos.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, 1941b, 2, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 95
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 90
suggested_refs: Eranos-Jahrbuch I/1933: Yoga und Meditation im Osten und im Westen

stops.name: Zürich, the yearbook at Rhein-Verlag
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the publisher; the month is a placeholder. Correction to the intake dossier, which cited Fröbe 1935 for the first volume: Sugden's bibliography shows that reference to be the Vorwort to Eranos-Jahrbuch II/1934, published 1935, the second yearbook. The first, Eranos-Jahrbuch I/1933, appeared in 1934. That she edited the first thirty volumes, covering conference years 1933-1961, is attested by English Wikipedia; the HathiTrust record cited in the dossier returned HTTP 403.
stops.campa: The papers go to Rhein-Verlag in Zürich and come back bound: Eranos-Jahrbuch I, the 1933 cycle, published in 1934, the first of thirty she will see through the press. She commissions, selects, edits, corrects and writes the preface. The lecturers' names go on the spine and hers goes in small type inside. From this year the conference is no longer an event on a shore; it is a series with a back catalogue, which is a different kind of object and a much harder one to end.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 90 and bibliography
suggested_refs: Eranos-Jahrbuch, Rhein-Verlag, Zürich, thirty volumes 1934-1962

stops.name: Moscia, the Archive founded
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding year by Sugden, p. 92, citing Fröbe 1936a; no month is given. The size, over 6,000 core images, is attested by the joint statement of 24 April 1948 and by AWARE.
stops.campa: In 1934 she founds the Eranos Archive for Research in Symbolism inside her own house: folders of photographs and photostats of religious and symbolic art, gathered by her, sorted by her, each folder labelled with the name of the archetype it holds. Nobody has commissioned it and nobody is funding it. It answers a practical problem the conferences created, that the lecturers keep describing images which nobody in the room can see. It answers a larger conviction too, one she never argues in public.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 92
Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: The Eranos Archive for Research in Symbolism, founded at Moscia 1934

stops.name: Crete, the collapse at the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and flagged as such by the source itself. The account comes from Fröbe's own letters of 1938 to Cary Baynes and to Dion Fortune, four years after the fact, and Sugden, p. 92, treats the trance as self-fashioning rather than as verified event, using the word allegedly. No source names the site within Crete; Knossos is a declared marker only. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: She goes to Crete looking for Great Mother imagery for the folders and comes back with something she cannot file. In letters written four years afterward she describes a waking trance that overwhelmed her with mythological imagery, and calls it an initiatory meeting with the Magna Mater. No source names where on the island it happened. Her most careful modern reader treats the whole account as a piece of self-fashioning rather than as testimony, and says so on the page.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, letter to Cary Baynes, 1938, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 96
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 92, 96
suggested_refs: Fröbe-Kapteyn to Cary Baynes, 1938, PP/CBA, Cary Baynes Archive, Wellcome Collection

stops.name: Moscia, the Visions
stops.date_confidence: attested, with an unresolved range. Sugden gives 315 drawings across twelve blue-bound albums, p. 100; the intake dossier's over 300 is corrected to the exact figure. The date range wobbles within the scholarship itself: Sugden's abstract says 1934-37, her body text 1934-38, and dated sheets run from Series I no. 9, March 1934, to no. 309, June 1937. The 1935 date orders the segment. The claim that Jung warned her against identification with archetypal forces is not what the source documents; what it documents is her own use of the phrase archetypal possession.
stops.campa: Back in the farmhouse she draws what she saw: three hundred and fifteen sheets in pencil, chalk pastel and mixed media on onion-skin paper, made by Jung's method of active imagination, dated by their maker from March 1934 onward. They are bound into twelve albums in blue and stay unpublished for ninety years. She writes that the encounter carried her to the edge of what she calls archetypal possession. Even the scholarship that counted the sheets cannot decide whether the series closes in 1937 or 1938.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 89, 92, 100
suggested_refs: The Blue Book, twelve albums, Eranos Foundation Archives, Ascona-Moscia, items such as OFK-V-001-022

stops.name: South Kensington, the letter to the Warburg Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested for the approach by Tevebring; no month is given. Coordinate corrected for anachronism: the intake pool pinned Woburn Square, where the Warburg moved only in 1958. From 1937 to 1958 the Institute occupied the Imperial Institute Buildings at South Kensington, and before that Thames House, so the South Kensington pin covers both the 1936 approach and the mid-1950s transfer.
stops.campa: In 1936 she writes to the Warburg Institute in London, proposing an enlarged relationship over the collecting of images. The approach opens a correspondence that will run for twenty years and end with her giving them everything. The library is Aby Warburg's, carried out of Hamburg in 1933 with its photographic collection intact, and it is the only institution in Europe doing to the history of art what she has been doing alone in a bedroom at Moscia: filing pictures by what they mean rather than by who made them.
sources: Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: The Warburg Institute Photographic Collection, Imperial Institute Buildings, South Kensington, 1937-1958

stops.name: Casa Eranos, the year of the Great Mother
stops.date_confidence: attested. The 1938 theme, the form and cult of the Great Mother, and the lecture titles Kult der Magna Mater and Die gnostische Vorstellung der Sophia are given by Sugden, pp. 91 and 93, citing Eranos-Jahrbuch V/1938 and the 1938 programme. Correction to the intake dossier, which said she delivered or organized these lectures: they are papers by invited speakers, her own contribution being the Vorwort, and she is nowhere recorded as an Eranos lecturer. The quote is that Vorwort, published 1939; Sugden renders the sense as her calling herself servant of a leading Idea, though the German is plural. The exact conference day is not recorded here.
stops.campa: For 1938 she sets the annual theme herself: the form and the cult of the Great Mother. The programme carries lectures on the cult of the Magna Mater and on the gnostic conception of Sophia, delivered by the men she invited. She writes the preface to the volume and nothing else in it. In twenty-eight years of Eranos she is nowhere recorded as a lecturer at her own conference, and in that preface she writes in the plural, placing everyone in the room, herself included, in the service of something none of them owns.
stops.quote: In der Eranos-Arbeit stehen wir im Dienste einer leitenden Idee. Unser Dank gebührt den Vortragenden, die mit uns dieser Idee dienen.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, Vorwort to Eranos-Jahrbuch V/1938: Vorträge über Gestalt und Kult der Grossen Mutter (Rhein-Verlag, 1939), 6, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 94 n. 8
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 91, 93, 94 n. 8
suggested_refs: Eranos-Jahrbuch V/1938: Vorträge über Gestalt und Kult der Grossen Mutter

stops.name: Moscia, the Americans arrive
stops.date_confidence: the introduction is attested by Tevebring, who places it during a Mellon visit to Switzerland in the late 1930s; the intake pool gave 1938 and named only the country, so the pin here is her own house and the date orders the segment. Her hope that Bollingen or Paul Mellon would buy the property and keep her as custodian, and its collapse with Mary Mellon's death in 1946, rests on Hakl 2013 and McGuire 1989, both of which returned HTTP 403 and could not be read directly.
stops.campa: Paul and Mary Conover Mellon come to Switzerland at the end of the thirties and are introduced to her. Mary Mellon's enthusiasm for Jung and her husband's money will shortly become the Bollingen Series, which carries the Ascona lectures into English and into American print for decades. Olga hopes for years that Bollingen or Paul Mellon will buy her property and keep her on as its custodian. Mary Mellon dies in 1946 and the hope dies with her. Where and how the introduction happened is not established.
sources: Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: William McGuire, Bollingen: An Adventure in Collecting the Past (Princeton, 1989)

stops.name: Athens, the gorgon at the Acropolis Museum
stops.date_confidence: attested that she acquired a photostat of a sixth-century BCE gorgoneion relief from the Acropolis Museum and filed it under Die Grosse Mutter: Die Gorgo, and that she complained of Greek archives where nothing is organised. The year is a placeholder within the 1930s and 1940s travelling period; no source dates the Athens visit.
stops.campa: She works the museum for the Archive and takes away a photostat of a sixth-century gorgoneion, the flat frontal face with the tongue out, which she files under Die Grosse Mutter: Die Gorgo. The Great Mother folder is where the terrifying goes as well as the nourishing, and she does not separate them. She is in her fifties and travelling alone, asking institutions that have no appointment with her for leave to photograph what they hold. Of the Greek collections she complains in a letter that nothing in them is organised.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025)
Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023

stops.name: Paris, the Bibliothèque nationale
stops.date_confidence: attested that she worked the Bibliothèque nationale in her research winters; the year is a placeholder. Coordinate corrected: the intake pool pinned 48.8656/2.3212, the Tuileries area, about 1.25 km off. In the 1930s and 1940s the Bibliothèque nationale meant the Richelieu site at 58 rue de Richelieu; Tolbiac opened only in 1996.
stops.campa: Winters are for the libraries. In Paris she works the Bibliothèque nationale in the rue de Richelieu for reproductions of religious and symbolic art, arguing sheet by sheet with the administration for the right to have things photographed. This is the daily substance of the Archive: permissions, fees, plates, postage, and a woman in her coat in a reading room in February. Every sheet she wins goes home to Moscia, into a folder named for an archetype. Her verdict on the librarians survives in her own English.
stops.quote: like demons on the books and manuscripts and becomes hostile when you force them to hand them over
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn on library administrators, quoted in Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
sources: Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: Bibliothèque nationale, site Richelieu, 58 rue de Richelieu, Paris

stops.name: Vatican Library, the Roman winter
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a name on the list of collections she worked, in English Wikipedia. No detailed account of her Roman work survives in any source consulted, and the year is a placeholder inside the 1930s and 1940s travelling period.
stops.campa: The Vatican Library is on the circuit too, one stop in a route that runs for years through the great collections of Europe and America. It appears in the record as a name on a list. What she takes from it is what she takes everywhere: photographs and photostats of religious art, ordered by subject, addressed to a farmhouse in Ticino. She travels on her own money, a private person with no institution behind her, asking curial librarians for their pictures. What she was shown, and what she was refused, no account records.
suggested_refs: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, photographic service records of the 1930s

stops.name: British Museum, London
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the collections she worked, in English Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder within the travelling period. The twelve boxes of Great Mother material are attested by the joint statement of 24 April 1948 as reported in Sugden, p. 99, which also corrects the intake dossier's conflation of boxes with the Archive's eighty-four folders.
stops.campa: The British Museum supplies its share of the folders. She is back in the city she was born in, close to sixty years on, working its collections as a foreigner with a Swiss address and a project no board has approved. The Archive is no longer an appendix to the conferences; it is the larger half of her working life, and it has begun to consume the house. The Great Mother material alone will grow to twelve boxes, and the photographs are stacked in the rooms where people live.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 99
suggested_refs: British Museum photographic service records, 1930s

stops.name: New York, the Morgan Library
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the American collections she visited, in English Wikipedia; the year is a placeholder. The duplicate American set that became ARAS is carried here with caution: the intake dossier dated the ARAS naming to 1960 and credited Olga, Mary Mellon and Jessie Fraser, but aras.org's own history page names Jessie E. Fraser and Jane Abbot Pratt, never Mary Conover Mellon, and gives no naming year. No ARAS stop is written, because the founding was not hers and she was not necessarily there.
stops.campa: In New York she works the Morgan among the American collections, on crossings that also carry her into the Bollingen circle and the money that will put the Ascona lectures into English. She crosses the Atlantic for pictures, in years when crossing the Atlantic is not a light undertaking. The images gathered here are copied twice: once for the folders at Moscia, once for a duplicate set that stays in America and becomes, after her lifetime, the Archive for Research in Archetypal Symbolism.
stops.quote: anyone who has come in contact with archetypal energy will know that he is up against something immensely powerful, immensely alive and creative, in fact the creative forces themselves. The lectures move around a centre, not represented by any personality but by an idea that we call Eranos. It stands for the Quest, or for the Self, or the Way of the Soul. Au fond, it escapes definition, being a paradox and an irrational thing.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, letter to Joseph Campbell, quoted in William McGuire, Bollingen (Princeton, 1989), 143, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 96
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 96
suggested_refs: Archive for Research in Archetypal Symbolism, 28 East 39th Street, New York

stops.name: Moscia, the war years and the filing problem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Sugden's Fröbe 1941b is the letter to Ximena de Angulo-Roelli of 21 September 1941, PP/CBA/C.1, Cary Baynes Archive, Wellcome Collection. Two corrections to the intake dossier: the typical synthetic creation of the new age line was dated there to 1939 and framed as pre-war, whereas it is wartime and from this letter; and both quotations were placed at the Warburg Institute, whereas in 1941 the Archive was still in her own house and reached London only in the 1950s. The quotation as the dossier carried it was also silently truncated, and the ellipsis is restored.
stops.campa: The frontiers close again, the speakers thin out, and Eranos goes on meeting on a shore a few hours from countries at war. In September 1941 she writes to Ximena de Angulo-Roelli about the Archive: how the folders are to be labelled, why each bound volume should carry the number of its folder, why an index is not yet needed and cross-indexing is beyond her altogether. In the same letter she calls Eranos a typical synthetic creation of the new age. Her reader glosses that as a beacon in the surrounding darkness.
stops.quote: On the inside of every volume of these compilations the number of the corresponding Mappe [folder] should be printed. The pictures will not need an extra index, at least not for a long time. Each Mappe will be labelled with the name of the archetype it contains...
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn to Ximena de Angulo-Roelli, 21 September 1941, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 98 n. 15
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 91, 98
suggested_refs: Fröbe-Kapteyn to Ximena de Angulo-Roelli, 21 September 1941, PP/CBA/C.1, Wellcome Collection

stops.name: Moscia, the count of the boxes
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the joint statement is Fröbe-Kapteyn et al., 24 April 1948, typescript, HS.1133:211, C. G. Jung Papers Collection, ETH Zürich, reported in Sugden, pp. 97 and 99. Correction to the intake dossier on two points: the statement says five years of winters, that is roughly 1943-48, not decades; and the twelve boxes and the eighty-four folders are different units, not twelve of eighty-four.
stops.campa: By April 1948 a statement she co-signs describes five years of winters in the great libraries and museums of Europe and America, and an Archive of over six thousand images in eighty-four folders, of which twelve boxes hold the Great Mother alone. The document speaks of her in the third person, as Frau Fröbe-Kapteyn, and it is the nearest thing to an institutional description of what she has actually been doing for fifteen years. No institution holds the collection. It is in her house, and she is sixty-six.
stops.quote: For the past five years, Frau Fröbe-Kapteyn has been working in the winters in the great libraries and museums of Europe and America. She is collecting photographs of religious art for the Eranos Archive of Images, which she also founded.
stops.quote_source: Joint statement co-signed by Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, 24 April 1948, HS.1133:211, ETH Zürich, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 97 n. 14
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 97, 99

stops.name: Casa Eranos, the last lecture of the man who made it famous
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date and pin are inherited byte-identical from jung.journey.json, the corpus's record of Jung's final Eranos lecture. Her preface to the volume for that cycle, Eranos-Jahrbuch XX/1951: Mensch und Zeit, was published by Rhein-Verlag in 1952; the intake pool cited the quotation as Eranos-Jahrbuch 1952, p. 7, which is the year of publication rather than of the cycle. Sugden gives the passage on p. 90, not p. 91 as the dossier had it.
stops.campa: Jung mounts the terrace lectern for the last time in August 1951 and speaks on synchronicity. She is sixty-nine, still setting the theme, still writing to the speakers, still carrying the papers away to the printer. Nineteen more conferences will follow without the man whose name brought half the audience, and she runs every one of them. The volume for this cycle, Eranos-Jahrbuch XX, appears the following year with her preface at the front of it, signed from Ascona.
stops.quote: We all serve the indestructible. Whether we know it or not [...] this service largely determines the quality and substance of the culture in the process of renewal.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, Vorwort to Eranos-Jahrbuch XX/1951: Mensch und Zeit (Rhein-Verlag, 1952), 7, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 90
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 90
suggested_refs: Eranos-Jahrbuch XX/1951: Mensch und Zeit

stops.name: South Kensington, the archive leaves the house
stops.date_confidence: contested date, re-weighted against the intake dossier. Three independent sources put the transfer in the middle 1950s: AWARE says mid-1950s; Sugden, p. 97, says in the 1950s; and Tevebring dates Erich Neumann's letter congratulating her that the photographs had left her house to 15 April 1955, which is the day used here. Only aras.org's history page says 1946, and the intake pool followed it and additionally misdated the Neumann letter to 1946. Both dates are recorded; neither is proven. The pin is South Kensington because the Institute moved to Woburn Square only in 1958.
stops.campa: In the middle fifties the Archive goes to London, to the Warburg Institute, over six thousand mounted photographs carried out of the rooms of a private house and into a public collection with a catalogue, a reading room and staff. Accounts differ over the year: one source places the gift in 1946, three put it in the fifties, and Erich Neumann's letter congratulating her that her room is once more fit for habitation is dated the fifteenth of April 1955. She had been sleeping among them.
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 97
Frederika Tevebring, 'Images from the Collective Unconscious,' Public Domain Review, 22 Feb 2023
suggested_refs: The Eranos Archive within the Warburg Institute Photographic Collection, London

stops.name: Casa Eranos, thirty volumes
stops.date_confidence: attested that she edited the first thirty Eranos yearbooks, covering conference years 1933-1961, per English Wikipedia; the month orders the segment. The lecturer roster is compiled from AWARE, English Wikipedia and Sugden, and from the corpus files wolfgang_pauli.journey.json, which stages a Kepler lecture at Eranos in the late 1940s, and martin_buber.journey.json. The letter quoted is dated March 1960 and reaches this file through Hakl 2013, which could not be read directly, as quoted in Sugden, p. 95.
stops.campa: By 1961 she has convened twenty-nine August meetings and edited thirty yearbooks, and the roster of people she has put on that terrace reads as a register of a century of comparative religion: Jung, Zimmer, Kerényi, Eliade, Corbin, Scholem, Suzuki, Portmann, Neumann, Martin Buber, and Wolfgang Pauli speaking on Kepler above the lake. She is seventy-nine. In a letter to Jung the year before, she sets down what the speakers keep telling her she is to them.
stops.quote: I am aware that my relationship to the [Eranos] speakers is always that of a mother to her son, as all the speakers are continually telling me, whether they understand anything of psychology or not.
stops.quote_source: Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn, letter to C. G. Jung, March 1960, in Hans Thomas Hakl, Eranos (McGill-Queen's, 2013), 295, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 95
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 95
suggested_refs: The first thirty Eranos-Jahrbücher, conference years 1933-1961

stops.name: Casa Gabriella, the death and the unopened albums
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English Wikipedia, AWARE and the ARAS newsletter. Two honest negatives: no source consulted gives a cause of death, and no source consulted locates a grave, tomb or cemetery marker of any kind. Adolf Portmann's succession is standard in the literature, but the intake pool cited Tevebring for it and Tevebring does not say it; the succession of Rudolf Ritsema is attested within the corpus by census_real_persons_2026-08-02.md, line 125.
stops.campa: She dies in the farmhouse on the twenty-fifth of April 1962, aged eighty, ten months after Jung. No source consulted gives a cause. The death is fixed to the day, and the body then leaves the record entirely. Eranos goes on without her, under Adolf Portmann and afterward Rudolf Ritsema. In the house the twelve blue albums stay where they were, unopened by anybody, until an exhibition at Locarno in 2024 and a facsimile the year after. Where she is buried, nobody has established.
stops.quote: When we, Adolf Portmann, Erich Neumann, Henry Corbin, Ernst Benz, Mircea Eliade, Karl Kerényi and many others—scholars of religion, psychologists, philosophers, physicists and biologists—were trying to play our part in Eranos, the figure of Olga Fröbe was crucial—she whom we always referred to among ourselves as 'the Great Mother.'
stops.quote_source: Gershom Scholem, 'Identifizierung und Distanz: Ein Rückblick,' Eranos Jahrbuch 48 (1979): 463, quoted in Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' 95 n. 9
sources: Chloë Sugden, 'Embodying the Great Mother,' Approaching Religion 15.2 (2025), 89, 95 n. 9
suggested_refs: Riccardo Bernardini, The Art of the Self: The Blue Book of Eranos Founder Olga Fröbe-Kapteyn (Chiron, 2025)
